title: Numbers and productivity trends of a Ciconia ciconia (White Stork) population in the face of a landfill closure
content:
Abstract
Landfills represent a peculiar source of food with an infinite and seasonally stable supply that many species have specialized in exploiting to the point of changing foraging or migratory behaviors. The recent European Landfill Directive requires member states of the European Union to implement regulations aimed at reducing organic waste and closing open landfills. Therefore, its application will lead to a drastic reduction in food resources, which will potentially reduce the number and general productivity of animal populations that have been benefiting from landfills. For this reason, this policy should be accompanied by a management plan for the affected species. We evaluate a buffer management of food (supplementary feeding) as a potential conservation measure on a Ciconia ciconia (White Stork) population facing the closure of a landfill, where the population had been feeding for more than 30 years. We analyze population trend and productivity metrics before and after the intervention (landfill closure + supplementary feeding). We found that the size of the population increased from 2009 to 2017 and gradually declined after 2017, coinciding with a decrease in population productivity, which was lower after than before the intervention, but followed the population trend. While nest and pair productivity were lower after the intervention, within-nest year-to-year change in productivity did not differ significantly before and after the intervention. Since the landfill closure and the supplementary feeding occurred simultaneously, their individual effects cannot be measured separately. The short post-closure period also limited our capacity to detect delayed or cumulative effects as long-term data are needed to establish the real effect of this type of management. Wildlife’s dependence should be addressed in the application of European landfill policies, promoting measures to alleviate the dependence of wildlife populations on this food source, taking into account each species and the particular local conditions.
